```{r}
#| label: inputs
#| include: false

# The price shock and its inputs (ICCT's Table 1 and the baseline market Q0) are computed here,
# because Results come before the appendices that show them.

# ICCT Table 1: extract page 5 as text and keep only the data rows (years 2028–2035)
pdf_path <- file.path(
  "data",
  "icct_biofuel_demand_report",
  "ID-450-Vegetable-Oil_research-brief_final.pdf"
)
page5 <- pdftools::pdf_text(pdf_path)[5]
lines <- stringr::str_trim(stringr::str_split(page5, "\n")[[1]])
data_lines <- stringr::str_subset(lines, "^20(2[89]|3[0-5])\\b")

# Each data row yields exactly 10 numeric tokens:
#   year, shipping demand, base target, fossil LNG %,
#   UCO-RD %, UCO-RD bl, VO-RD %, VO-RD bl, UCO demand bl, VO demand bl
nums <- stringr::str_extract_all(data_lines, "[0-9]+\\.?[0-9]*")
mat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(nums, function(x) as.numeric(x[seq_len(10)])))

icct_table_1 <- tibble::as_tibble(mat, .name_repair = "minimal")
names(icct_table_1) <- c(
  "year",
  "shipping_energy_demand_ej",
  "base_target_trajectory_gco2e_mj",
  "fossil_lng_pct",
  "ucord_pct_energy_demand",
  "ucord_billion_liters",
  "vord_pct_energy_demand",
  "vord_billion_liters",
  "uco_demand_billion_liters",
  "vo_demand_billion_liters"
)

icct_table_1 <- icct_table_1 |>
  dplyr::mutate(year = as.integer(year)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year)

# Saved for the setup chunk, which needs the 2035 VO-RD energy for the ILUC calculation.
utils::write.csv(icct_table_1, file.path("data", "derived", "icct_table_1.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Q0: world production of the four oils, USDA PSD
psd_zip_path <- file.path("data", "usda_psd_oilseeds", "psd_oilseeds_csv.zip")
psd <- utils::read.csv(unz(psd_zip_path, "psd_oilseeds.csv"))

q0_market_year <- 2024 # marketing year 2024/25

psd_four_oils <- psd |>
  dplyr::filter(
    Commodity_Description %in%
      c("Oil, Palm", "Oil, Soybean", "Oil, Rapeseed", "Oil, Sunflowerseed"),
    Attribute_Description == "Production",
    Market_Year == q0_market_year
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    production_mt = sum(Value) / 1000, # reported in 1000 MT
    .by = Commodity_Description
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(production_mt))
q0_mt <- sum(psd_four_oils$production_mt) # ~204 Mt

# Price shock: Q0 in billion liters at 0.92 kg/L, ICCT's own soy-oil conversion
# (12.4 Mt = 13.5 billion L, ICCT Table A1).
oil_density_kg_l <- 0.92
q0_billion_liters <- q0_mt / oil_density_kg_l # ~221 billion L

# %ΔP_t = (D_t / Q0) * M, as a percent, with the central multiplier and at the low and high ends.
# beyond_marginal flags years where the shift exceeds 25% of the market, outside the regime where
# the approximation is reliable.
price_shock <- icct_table_1 |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    year,
    vo_demand_billion_liters,
    demand_share_pct = 100 * vo_demand_billion_liters / q0_billion_liters,
    pct_delta_p_rs = demand_share_pct * m_rs,
    pct_delta_p_rs_low = demand_share_pct * rs_low$m,
    pct_delta_p_rs_high = demand_share_pct * rs_high$m,
    beyond_marginal = demand_share_pct > 25
  )
share_2035 <- price_shock$demand_share_pct[price_shock$year == 2035]

# Hand-off to the land-use model (full precision, no rounding). 01_prepare_data.R reads
# vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv: the central shock and the low and high ends of Roberts &
# Schlenker's estimates. The central elasticities are saved alongside.
handoff_2035 <- price_shock |>
  dplyr::filter(year == 2035) |>
  dplyr::mutate(eps_s = eps_s_rs, eps_d = eps_d_rs)

dir.create(file.path("data", "derived"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
utils::write.csv(
  handoff_2035,
  file.path("data", "derived", "vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
utils::write.csv(
  price_shock,
  file.path("data", "derived", "vegetable_oil_price_shock.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

# The setup chunk read this file for the report's text, before this render rewrote it. If it was out
# of date, that text used old numbers: stop so the report is rendered again.
if (!isTRUE(all.equal(shock_2035, as.data.frame(handoff_2035), check.attributes = FALSE))) {
  stop("vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv was out of date and has been rewritten. Render again.")
}
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Preliminary and exploratory

This is an exploratory prototype analysis. It looks at the potential of using emLab's land-use model to forecast the indirect land-use change (ILUC) impacts of increasing biofuel demand, using ICCT's projected vegetable-oil demand for marine biofuel as a test case. Its results provide a first look at the likely scale of these impacts, and can be compared with published ILUC values. However, they should not be used as an ILUC factor for policy, regulation, or carbon accounting, as a forecast of vegetable-oil prices, or to attribute emissions to specific countries.

The main caveats are:

- The price shock, which drives all of the results that follow, comes from a simple formula that is meant for small changes in demand. However, vegetable-oil demand for marine biofuel would equal `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of current world vegetable-oil production. The formula also uses Roberts & Schlenker's supply and demand elasticities, which were estimated for staple crops rather than vegetable oils.
- The price shock raises the palm oil price to `r fmt1(1 + shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs / 100)` times its 2020 level. Since the land-use model was estimated using 2001–2020 data, its response at prices this high is untested. The model also predicts forest clearing but not what the cleared land is then used for, and we count all of the additional clearing as ILUC.
- Country-level results are the least reliable part of the analysis. We apply the same world price change in every country, and the land-use model's broad crop zones shift some of the palm response to Central Africa.
- We only count carbon in forest biomass (i.e., not peat or soil carbon), and the model does not include rapeseed or sunflower. Both of these make our ILUC values too low. On the other hand, we make no adjustment for the value of soybean meal, which makes them too high.
- Our sensitivity analysis only captures the spread across Roberts & Schlenker's six specifications of supply and demand elasticities. It does not capture these other uncertainties.

The [Caveats](#sec-caveats) section provides the full list.
:::

## Executive summary

In April 2025, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) approved a draft Net-Zero Framework that would set greenhouse-gas intensity targets for the fuel used by large ships, and would charge ships that miss those targets [@sturrup2026, p. 1; @seber2025, pp. 1–2]. The framework has not yet been adopted. A vote was postponed in October 2025, and a vote could happen as soon as 4 December 2026 [@carbonbrief2026; @abs2026mepc84, p. 4]. The framework only counts the direct life-cycle emissions of fuels. ILUC, which is the forest cleared elsewhere when biofuel demand raises crop prices, is instead handled through a qualitative approach [@imo2024lca, paras. 4.12–4.13]. ICCT projects that the least-cost compliance pathway relies heavily on renewable diesel made from virgin vegetable oil (VO-RD), which would reach 46% of shipping energy by 2035 [@seber2025, p. 4 and Table 1, p. 5].

This analysis finds a central ILUC estimate for marine VO-RD of `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 25))` g CO₂ per MJ, when spread over `r headline_years` years of fuel use (`r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 20))` over 20 years and `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 30))` over 30 years). Our sensitivity analysis, described below, gives a range of `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_low", 25))` to `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_high", 25))` g CO₂/MJ (@tbl-iluc-sensitivity). Adding VO-RD's direct life-cycle emissions of `r vord_direct_ci` g CO₂e/MJ [@seber2025, p. 6] gives a total of `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs", 25))` g/MJ, compared with a fossil baseline of `r fossil_baseline_ci`.

ICCT's projection requires about `r fmt0(shock_2035$vo_demand_billion_liters)` billion liters of virgin vegetable oil per year by 2035 [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5], which is `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of current world production of palm, soybean, rapeseed, and sunflower oil. Demand at this scale would raise vegetable-oil prices, and higher prices make it more profitable to clear forest for oil palm and soybeans. How much prices rise depends on how much farmers expand production and how much other buyers reduce their consumption as prices increase. Supply and demand elasticities measure these two responses. For our central estimate, we use Roberts & Schlenker's widely used central estimates for staple crops, a supply elasticity of `r fmt_el(eps_s_rs)` and a demand elasticity of `r fmt_el(eps_d_rs)` [@roberts2013, Table 1, p. 2279], and use a simple supply-and-demand formula to translate the demand into a price shock. The resulting shock raises palm oil prices by `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`% and soybean prices by `r fmt0(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%, since oil makes up about 35% of a soybean's value [@janzen2025, Fig. 2]. We then run emLab's land-use model, which translates prices into forest loss, both with and without these price increases. Finally, we divide the additional forest carbon loss by the energy from `r headline_years` years of VO-RD use. We refer to this as our primary scenario.

We also conduct a sensitivity analysis by repeating these steps with the two of Roberts & Schlenker's six specifications that give the smallest and largest price response (i.e., the most and least responsive supply and demand). These two specifications form the low and high bounds of our range. Across Roberts & Schlenker's six specifications, the 2035 price shock therefore ranges from `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_low)`% to `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_high)`%, and the resulting `r headline_years`-year ILUC value ranges from `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_low", 25))` to `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_high", 25))` g CO₂/MJ.

In the primary scenario, the emLab model predicts that an additional `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", 2035, "area_loss") / 1e6)` Mha of forest would be cleared within 15 years compared with business as usual (BAU), releasing `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", 2035, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂. Over the model's full `r n_years`-year run, the totals are `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", final_year, "area_loss") / 1e6)` Mha and `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂. The palm oil price increase causes `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["palm"]] / sum(crop_split))`% of the additional loss. `r sub("^the ", "The ", the_country(rs_final$country[1]))` and `r the_country(rs_final$country[2])` account for `r fmt0(100 * sum(rs_final$share[1:2]))`% of the additional loss, although the country-level results are the least reliable part of the analysis.

For comparison, ICCT has previously used an ILUC value of 62 g CO₂e/MJ [@sturrup2026, p. 10], and @chen2026 [Table 1, p. 13] estimate 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ for palm oil. Our value is `r vs_benchmarks(il("vo_rs", 25))`. Both benchmarks, like ours, are ILUC values alone. ICCT's 62 should therefore be compared with our `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 25))`, rather than with our total of `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs", 25))`. Since we only count forest biomass carbon, the closest benchmark is Chen et al.'s biomass carbon value alone, which is `r chen_biomass_iluc` g CO₂e/MJ (peat adds another 47.5) [@chen2026, Table 1, p. 13]. While our value is close to theirs, the two estimates come from different places. Only `r fmt1(im_iluc)` g/MJ of our value comes from Indonesia and Malaysia, the two countries they study, while `r fmt1(drc_iluc)` comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Overall, this prototype shows that emLab's land-use model can be used to estimate the ILUC impacts of increasing biofuel demand, and that it produces values on a similar scale to published estimates. However, the results depend heavily on the price shock, and the country-level results in particular should be interpreted with caution.

## Approach {#sec-approach}

ILUC occurs when biofuel demand raises crop prices, and these higher prices lead to forest being cleared for farmland elsewhere. These emissions fall outside of the fuel's own supply chain, so a fuel mix can meet the framework's greenhouse-gas intensity targets on paper while still adding emissions that are not counted. @fig-steps shows how we estimate these emissions, and who supplies each step.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-steps
%%| fig-cap: "From the IMO Net-Zero Framework to an ILUC carbon intensity: the steps, and who supplies each."
flowchart LR
  A["IMO Net-Zero Framework"] --> F["Marine VO-RD demand<br/><i>ICCT cost-optimization</i>"]
  F --> B["Virgin vegetable-oil demand<br/><i>1.22 kg oil per kg renewable diesel</i>"]
  B --> C["Vegetable-oil price shock<br/><i>this report</i>"]
  C --> D["Forest loss by country<br/><i>emLab land-use model</i>"]
  D --> E["ILUC carbon intensity<br/><i>this report</i>"]
```

The analysis consists of five steps:

1. Translate ICCT's 2035 vegetable-oil demand into a price shock, using Roberts & Schlenker's central supply and demand elasticities.
2. Translate the price shock into prices for the emLab model's crops.
3. Run the model with baseline prices and with shocked prices (both with a carbon price of zero), and take the difference in forest loss.
4. Spread the additional emissions over the fuel used, giving a value in g CO₂ per MJ.
5. For the sensitivity analysis, repeat steps 1–4 using the low and high ends of Roberts & Schlenker's estimates.

Similar to Chen et al., we estimate how much the demand shift raises prices, and then use an econometric land-use model to translate prices into forest loss. This differs from approaches that assume a fixed ILUC factor. [Appendix A](#background) provides more background on the IMO Net-Zero Framework and published ILUC estimates, and [Appendix B](#methods-and-assumptions) describes each step in detail.

## Results

This section presents the results in the same order as the steps of the analysis. We first show how ICCT's projected vegetable-oil demand for marine biofuel translates into a vegetable-oil price shock. We then show the additional forest loss that emLab's land-use model predicts from this price shock, globally and by country and crop, in terms of both carbon and forest area. Finally, we convert the additional forest carbon loss into an ILUC carbon intensity for VO-RD, and show how this value changes in our sensitivity analysis.

### Vegetable-oil price shock {#sec-results-price}

ICCT projects that virgin vegetable-oil demand for marine biofuel starts in `r min(price_shock$year[price_shock$vo_demand_billion_liters > 0])` and grows to `r fmt0(shock_2035$vo_demand_billion_liters)` billion liters by 2035 (@fig-price-shock, left). By 2035, this is equal to `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of current world production of the four major vegetable oils. Using Roberts & Schlenker's central elasticities, this demand raises vegetable-oil prices by `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`% in 2035 (@fig-price-shock, right). At the low and high ends of their estimates, the 2035 price shock ranges from `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_low)`% to `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_high)`%. From `r min(price_shock$year[price_shock$beyond_marginal])` onward, this demand is more than 25% of the market, which is beyond the range where the simple price-shock formula is reliable.

```{r}
#| label: fig-price-shock
#| column: body-outset
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "Vegetable oil for marine biofuel projected by ICCT (left) and the resulting change in vegetable-oil prices (right), by year. The price change uses Roberts & Schlenker's central elasticities (line), and the band spans the low and high ends of their estimates. The land-use model runs use the 2035 values."

# Two panels sharing the year axis: demand (bars) and the price change it implies (line and band).
panel_names <- c(
  "Vegetable oil for marine biofuel (billion L a year)",
  "Change in vegetable-oil price (%)"
)
demand_panel <- price_shock |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    year,
    panel = factor(panel_names[1], levels = panel_names),
    value = vo_demand_billion_liters
  )
price_panel <- price_shock |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    year,
    panel = factor(panel_names[2], levels = panel_names),
    value = pct_delta_p_rs,
    low = pct_delta_p_rs_low,
    high = pct_delta_p_rs_high
  )

ggplot2::ggplot(mapping = ggplot2::aes(year, value)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(data = demand_panel, fill = col_primary, width = 0.65) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(data = price_panel, ggplot2::aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), fill = col_range, alpha = 0.6) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(data = price_panel, colour = col_primary, linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = price_panel, shape = 21, size = 2.8, stroke = 0.8,
    colour = col_surface, fill = col_primary
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(panel), scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(clip = "off") + # keeps the 2028 point at 0% from being cut in half
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = price_shock$year) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Marine biofuel demand for vegetable oil, and the resulting price shock",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-market-2035
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Roberts & Schlenker's demand curve for vegetable oil before and after the 2035 demand from marine biofuel, with their supply curve, using their central elasticities. Prices are shown as an index, with today's price equal to 100. The points mark today's market and the 2035 price shock run through the model, labeled with the percentage price change."

# The vegetable-oil market in 2035: demand before and after ICCT's marine demand D, against supply.
# All curves use the price-shock formula's linear approximation, %dQ = eps x %dP. Prices are plotted
# as an index (today = 100), i.e., 100 + %dP.
shock_rs <- price_shock$pct_delta_p_rs[price_shock$year == 2035]
d_mt <- price_shock$vo_demand_billion_liters[price_shock$year == 2035] * oil_density_kg_l
extra_supply_mt <- eps_s_rs * shock_rs / 100 * q0_mt

curve_names <- c(
  paste0("Demand today (ε = ", fmt_el(eps_d_rs), ")"),
  "Demand with 2035 marine biofuel",
  paste0("Supply (ε = ", fmt_el(eps_s_rs), ")")
)
p_grid <- seq(-50, 600, by = 10)
market_curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[1], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_d_rs * p_grid / 100)),
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[2], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_d_rs * p_grid / 100) + d_mt),
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[3], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_s_rs * p_grid / 100))
)
market_curves$curve <- factor(market_curves$curve, levels = curve_names)
equilibria <- data.frame(
  q = q0_mt + c(0, extra_supply_mt),
  p = c(0, shock_rs),
  label = c("Today", paste0("+", fmt0(shock_rs), "%"))
)

ggplot2::ggplot(market_curves, ggplot2::aes(q, 100 + p, colour = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = equilibria, ggplot2::aes(q, 100 + p), inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 21, size = 3, fill = "#0b0b0b", colour = col_surface, stroke = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(
    data = equilibria, ggplot2::aes(q, 100 + p, label = label), inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = -0.3, size = 3.4, colour = "#0b0b0b"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    values = stats::setNames(c("#8f8d86", "#0b0b0b", col_primary), curve_names),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = stats::setNames(c("22", "solid", "solid"), curve_names), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), breaks = seq(100, 700, 100)) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(150, 350, 50)) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(130, 360), ylim = c(50, 700), expand = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "The world vegetable-oil market in 2035",
    x = "Vegetable oil (Mt a year)",
    y = "Vegetable-oil price (index, today = 100)"
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

@fig-market-2035 shows the 2035 vegetable-oil market, including Roberts & Schlenker's demand curve before and after the `r fmt0(d_mt)` Mt of vegetable oil that ICCT projects for marine biofuel in 2035, as well as their supply curve. Prices rise until the additional supply and the reduced consumption by other buyers together cover the demand from ships. This requires a price increase of `r fmt0(shock_rs)`%, which adds `r fmt0(extra_supply_mt)` Mt per year of supply and reduces other buyers' consumption by `r fmt0(d_mt - extra_supply_mt)` Mt. Note that this is not a forecast. The demand shift is far outside the range where the linear formula holds, and with elasticities this small, the result depends mostly on the assumed shape of the curves. Across Roberts & Schlenker's six specifications, the multiplier ranges from `r fmt1(rs_low$m)` to `r fmt1(rs_high$m)`, which puts the price shock between `r fmt0(share_2035 * rs_low$m)`% and `r fmt0(share_2035 * rs_high$m)`% (@tbl-price-shock-check). We use these 2035 price shocks as the inputs to the land-use model runs in the next section.

### Forest loss {#sec-results-forest}

We run emLab's land-use model with and without the 2035 price shock, and compare the two runs. Additional forest loss is the difference in forest between the BAU run and the shocked run. Since it is cumulative, the final model year gives the total over the entire simulation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-forest-loss-global

horizons <- c(2035, 2050, final_year)
global_table <- global_loss |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_rs", year %in% horizons) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Years after shock" = global_table$year - min(lum$year),
    "Gt CO₂" = global_table$carbon_loss / 1e9,
    "Mha" = global_table$area_loss / 1e6,
    "% of BAU forest carbon" = 100 * global_table$carbon_loss / global_table$carbon_bau,
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Cumulative additional forest loss relative to BAU in the primary scenario, all countries."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-loss-timeseries
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative additional forest carbon loss relative to BAU in the primary scenario, over the full run."

global_ts <- global_loss |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_rs") |>
  dplyr::mutate(years_after_shock = year - min(lum$year), carbon_gt = carbon_loss / 1e9)

ggplot2::ggplot(global_ts, ggplot2::aes(years_after_shock, carbon_gt)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = col_primary, linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 150, 25), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Cumulative additional forest carbon loss relative to BAU",
    x = "Years after the price shock",
    y = expression("Gt CO"[2])
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

About half of the full-run loss (`r fmt0(100 * gl("vo_rs", 2035, "carbon_loss") / gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss"))`%) happens in the first 15 years.

#### Where the loss falls

```{r}

Gray countries have no additional loss (no oil palm or soybean area in the model) or are not in the model. Where the model pools neighboring countries into one region, each member shows the region's total; all such regions lose less than 1 Mt CO₂."

#### By country and crop

To split the loss by crop, we ran the primary price shock on palm alone and on soybeans alone. Palm accounts for `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["palm"]] / sum(crop_split))`% of the additional loss, while soybeans account for `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["soy"]] / sum(crop_split))`%. The two single-crop runs add up to the combined run within `r formatC(abs(interaction_pct), format = "f", digits = 2)`%, meaning the interaction between them is negligible.

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-loss-by-crop
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative additional forest carbon loss over the full horizon in the primary scenario, by country, split between the palm-only and soy-only runs."

top_n <- 12
top_countries <- rs_final$country[seq_len(top_n)]
other_label <- sprintf("Other %d countries", sum(rs_final$carbon_loss > 0) - top_n)

crop_by_country <- country_final |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("vo_rs_palm", "vo_rs_soy")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    label = ifelse(country %in% top_countries, country, other_label),
    crop = ifelse(scenario == "vo_rs_palm", "Oil palm", "Soybeans")
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mt = sum(carbon_loss) / 1e6, .by = c(label, crop)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(c(top_countries, other_label))))
bar_totals <- crop_by_country |> dplyr::summarise(mt = sum(mt), .by = label)

ggplot2::ggplot(crop_by_country, ggplot2::aes(mt, label)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(
    ggplot2::aes(fill = crop),
    position = ggplot2::position_stack(reverse = TRUE), # palm first, from zero
    width = 0.62, colour = col_surface, linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = bar_totals, ggplot2::aes(label = fmt0(mt)), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2, colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = col_crop, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Additional forest carbon loss by country and crop",
    subtitle = "Primary scenario, full horizon",
    x = expression("Mt CO"[2]),
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_report() +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-forest-loss-country
#| tbl-cap: "Cumulative additional forest loss relative to BAU in the primary scenario over the full horizon, by country. Palm and soybean columns are the single-crop runs."

country_table <- country_final |>
  dplyr::filter(carbon_loss > 0) |>
  dplyr::select(country, scenario, carbon_loss, area_loss, area_bau, share)
by_scenario <- function(scn, ...) {
  country_table |> dplyr::filter(scenario == scn) |> dplyr::select(country, ...)
}
country_table <- by_scenario("vo_rs", carbon_loss, area_loss, area_bau, share) |>
  dplyr::left_join(by_scenario("vo_rs_palm", carbon_palm = carbon_loss), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::left_join(by_scenario("vo_rs_soy", carbon_soy = carbon_loss), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    country,
    carbon_mt = carbon_loss / 1e6,
    palm_mt = dplyr::coalesce(carbon_palm, 0) / 1e6,
    soy_mt = dplyr::coalesce(carbon_soy, 0) / 1e6,
    area_kha = area_loss / 1e3,
    share_pct = 100 * share,
    pct_of_bau_area = 100 * area_loss / area_bau
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(carbon_mt))

DT::datatable(
  country_table,
  rownames = FALSE,
  colnames = c(
    "Country",
    "Mt CO₂",
    "of which palm",
    "of which soybeans",
    "Thousand ha",
    "Share of total (%)",
    "% of country's BAU forest"
  ),
  options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)
) |>
  DT::formatRound(c("carbon_mt", "palm_mt", "soy_mt", "area_kha", "share_pct", "pct_of_bau_area"), digits = 1)
```

`r sum(rs_final$carbon_loss > 0)` countries lose some additional forest. However, `r the_country(rs_final$country[1])`, `r the_country(rs_final$country[2])`, and `r the_country(rs_final$country[3])` account for `r fmt0(100 * sum(rs_final$share[1:3]))`% of the total. Only grid cells that grow oil palm or soybeans respond, since those are the only crop prices that change.

Since cleared forest never grows back in the model, forest that is cleared early in a shocked run can instead be cleared later in the BAU run. In Malaysia, for example, the additional loss peaks at `r fmt0(mys$peak / 1e6)` Mt CO₂ in model year `r mys$peak_year` and falls to `r fmt0(mys$final / 1e6)` Mt CO₂ by `r final_year`. Overall, `r n_narrowing` countries end more than 5% below their peak. Globally, the additional loss is still increasing at the end of the run. The ILUC estimates only count loss within the accounting period, so this late catch-up does not affect them.

```{r}
#| label: area-numbers
#| include: false

# Numbers for the text: how area and carbon rank the countries, and carbon per hectare among the ten
# countries with the most additional area cleared.
carbon_rank <- stats::setNames(seq_len(nrow(rs_final)), rs_final$country)
top10_area <- area_final[seq_len(10), ]
lowest_density <- top10_area[which.min(top10_area$t_per_ha), ]
highest_density <- top10_area[which.max(top10_area$t_per_ha), ]
# Countries among the top_n by area that rank at least three places higher by area than by carbon.
rank_up <- area_final$country[seq_len(top_n)][
  seq_len(top_n) + 3 <= carbon_rank[area_final$country[seq_len(top_n)]]
]
rank_up_text <- if (length(rank_up) > 0) {
  paste0(
    " By area, ", knitr::combine_words(the_country(rank_up)),
    if (length(rank_up) == 1) " ranks" else " rank", " at least three places higher than by carbon."
  )
} else {
  ""
}
```

Over the full horizon, the emLab model predicts that `r fmt1(sum(rs_final$area_loss) / 1e6)` Mha more forest would be cleared in the primary scenario than in BAU. `r sub("^the ", "The ", the_country(area_final$country[1]))`, `r the_country(area_final$country[2])`, and `r the_country(area_final$country[3])` account for `r fmt0(100 * sum(area_final$area_share[1:3]))`% of this area. Area and carbon rank countries differently because the carbon density of the cleared forest varies. On average, the additional forest cleared holds `r fmt0(sum(rs_final$carbon_loss) / sum(rs_final$area_loss))` t CO₂ per hectare. Among the ten countries with the most additional forest cleared, this ranges from `r fmt0(lowest_density$t_per_ha)` in `r the_country(lowest_density$country)` to `r fmt0(highest_density$t_per_ha)` in `r the_country(highest_density$country)`.`r rank_up_text` The country-level area results have the same caveats as the carbon results ([Caveats](#sec-caveats)).

### ILUC carbon intensity {#sec-results-iluc}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-iluc

iluc_central <- iluc[iluc$scenario == "vo_rs", ]
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Accounting period (years)" = iluc_central$years,
    "Additional loss (Gt CO₂)" = iluc_central$carbon_loss / 1e9,
    "ILUC (g CO₂/MJ)" = iluc_central$g_per_mj,
    "VO-RD total (g CO₂e/MJ)" = vord_direct_ci + iluc_central$g_per_mj,
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = c(0, 2, 1, 1),
  caption = paste0(
    "ILUC carbon intensity of VO-RD in the primary scenario for each accounting period, using ",
    fmt1(vord_mj_2035 / 1e12), " EJ of VO-RD a year. VO-RD total adds the direct 42.3 g CO₂e/MJ ",
    "[@seber2025, p. 6]; the fossil baseline is 93.3 [@seber2025, p. 1]."
  )
)
```

Over the `r headline_years`-year headline accounting period, ILUC is `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 25))` g CO₂/MJ. The 30-year value of `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 30))` is the most appropriate comparison with ICCT's 62 g CO₂e/MJ, which is based on a 2020–2050 window. Both benchmarks (i.e., ICCT's 62 and Chen et al.'s 84.1) are ILUC values alone, so they should be compared with these values rather than with totals that include VO-RD's direct `r vord_direct_ci` g CO₂e/MJ. Our values only count forest biomass carbon, so they leave out the 47.5 g CO₂e/MJ that Chen et al. add for peat and the 7.3 g CO₂e/MJ for non-peat soil. Their biomass carbon value alone is `r chen_biomass_iluc`, before a credit of −29.4 for the carbon taken up by the new palms [@chen2026, Table 1, p. 13].

```{r}
#| label: fig-iluc-by-country
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: !expr paste0("Each country's contribution to the primary scenario's ", headline_years, "-year ILUC value, split between the palm-only and soy-only runs.")

# Contributions to the headline ILUC estimate: each country's additional loss after
# headline_years years in the palm-only and soy-only runs, in g CO2 per MJ of VO-RD.
iluc_year <- min(lum$year) + headline_years
iluc_by_country <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(year == iluc_year, scenario %in% c("bau", "vo_rs_palm", "vo_rs_soy")) |>
  dplyr::select(country, scenario, forest_carbon_tco2) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    palm = forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "bau"] - forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "vo_rs_palm"],
    soy = forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "bau"] - forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "vo_rs_soy"],
    .by = country
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(c(palm, soy), \(x) x * 1e6 / (headline_years * vord_mj_2035)),
    total = palm + soy
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(total))

iluc_top_n <- 10
iluc_top <- iluc_by_country$country[seq_len(iluc_top_n)]
iluc_other <- sprintf("Other %d countries", sum(iluc_by_country$total > 0) - iluc_top_n)
iluc_plot <- iluc_by_country |>
  dplyr::mutate(label = ifelse(country %in% iluc_top, country, iluc_other)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(`Oil palm` = sum(palm), Soybeans = sum(soy), .by = label)
iluc_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(label = iluc_plot$label, crop = "Oil palm", g_per_mj = iluc_plot$`Oil palm`),
  data.frame(label = iluc_plot$label, crop = "Soybeans", g_per_mj = iluc_plot$Soybeans)
)
iluc_plot$label <- factor(iluc_plot$label, levels = rev(c(iluc_top, iluc_other)))
iluc_totals <- iluc_plot |> dplyr::summarise(g_per_mj = sum(g_per_mj), .by = label)

ggplot2::ggplot(iluc_plot, ggplot2::aes(g_per_mj, label)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(
    ggplot2::aes(fill = crop),
    position = ggplot2::position_stack(reverse = TRUE),
    width = 0.62, colour = col_surface, linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = iluc_totals, ggplot2::aes(label = fmt1(g_per_mj)), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2, colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = col_crop, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Contributions to the ILUC estimate by country and crop",
    subtitle = paste0("Primary scenario, ", headline_years, "-year accounting period"),
    x = expression("g CO"[2] * " per MJ of VO-RD"),
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_report() +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Two countries, `r the_country(iluc_by_country$country[1])` and `r the_country(iluc_by_country$country[2])`, contribute `r fmt1(sum(iluc_by_country$total[1:2]))` of the `r fmt1(sum(iluc_by_country$total))` g CO₂/MJ total, and the palm price increase accounts for `r fmt0(100 * sum(iluc_by_country$palm) / sum(iluc_by_country$total))`% of the total. Indonesia and Malaysia, the only countries that Chen et al. study, contribute `r fmt1(im_iluc)` g CO₂/MJ, compared with their `r chen_biomass_iluc` g CO₂e/MJ from biomass carbon.

### Sensitivity analysis {#sec-results-sensitivity}

For the sensitivity analysis, we repeat every step, from the price shock to ILUC, using the two Roberts & Schlenker specifications that give the smallest and largest price multiplier (@tbl-price-shock-check). These two specifications form the low and high bounds of our range.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-iluc-sensitivity

# The primary scenario and the runs at the low and high ends of Roberts & Schlenker's estimates: their
# Table 1 specifications with the smallest and largest multiplier (setup chunk), each run through the
# model like the central case.
sens <- data.frame(
  case = c(
    paste0("Low end: smallest multiplier (", rs_low$spec, ")"), "Central values (primary scenario)",
    paste0("High end: largest multiplier (", rs_high$spec, ")")
  ),
  scenario = c("vo_rs_low", "vo_rs", "vo_rs_high"),
  eps_s = c(rs_low$eps_s, eps_s_rs, rs_high$eps_s),
  eps_d = c(rs_low$eps_d, eps_d_rs, rs_high$eps_d),
  shock = c(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_low, shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs, shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_high)
)
sens_il <- function(yrs) vapply(sens$scenario, il, numeric(1), yrs = yrs)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Roberts & Schlenker estimate" = sens$case,
    "Supply elasticity" = fmt_el(sens$eps_s),
    "Demand elasticity" = fmt_el(sens$eps_d),
    "Price shock, 2035" = paste0(fmt0(sens$shock), "%"),
    "ILUC, 20 years" = fmt1(sens_il(20)),
    "ILUC, 25 years" = fmt1(sens_il(25)),
    "ILUC, 30 years" = fmt1(sens_il(30)),
    check.names = FALSE,
    row.names = NULL
  ),
  align = "lrrrrrr",
  caption = paste(
    "ILUC carbon intensity of VO-RD (g CO₂/MJ) with Roberts & Schlenker's central values and at the low and",
    "high ends of their estimates: the two of their six Table 1 specifications with the smallest and largest",
    "multiplier [@roberts2013, p. 2279], which form the bounds of our sensitivity analysis. All three are run",
    "through the emLab model. IV is instrumental variables and 3SLS is three-stage least squares."
  )
)
```

Across Roberts & Schlenker's six specifications, the `r headline_years`-year ILUC value ranges from `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_low", 25))` to `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_high", 25))` g CO₂/MJ. This is `r fmt0(100 * (1 - il("vo_rs_low", 25) / il("vo_rs", 25)))`% below and `r fmt0(100 * (il("vo_rs_high", 25) / il("vo_rs", 25) - 1))`% above the central value, which is roughly in line with the change in the price shock (`r fmt0(100 * (1 - shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_low / shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs))`% below and `r fmt0(100 * (shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_high / shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs - 1))`% above). Including VO-RD's direct `r vord_direct_ci` g CO₂e/MJ, the total ranges from `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs_low", 25))` to `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs_high", 25))` g/MJ, compared with a fossil baseline of `r fossil_baseline_ci`. Across all three accounting periods, the range is `r fmt1(min(iluc$g_per_mj))` to `r fmt1(max(iluc$g_per_mj))` g CO₂/MJ.

This range only captures the spread across Roberts & Schlenker's specifications. It does not capture the other uncertainties described in the [Caveats](#sec-caveats) section, such as the linear approximation, the use of staple-crop elasticities for vegetable oils, and the carbon pools we do not count.

## Caveats {#sec-caveats}

- The price shock comes from a linear approximation applied to a demand shift equal to `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of the market, so the true price response is probably larger. In addition, Roberts & Schlenker's elasticities are for staple calories (i.e., maize, wheat, rice, and soybeans), rather than vegetable oils.
- The price shock takes its supply response from Roberts & Schlenker, which includes every source of additional supply (e.g., higher yields, other crops, and new farmland regardless of whether it was previously forest). However, the emLab model translates prices into forest clearing only, so we do not count any land-use change outside of forests.
- The primary price shock raises the palm oil price to `r fmt1(1 + shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs / 100)` times its 2020 level. The emLab model was estimated using 2001–2020 data, so its response at prices this high is untested.
- The model predicts forest clearing, but not what the cleared land is used for. We count all of the additional clearing as ILUC.
- Country-level results are the weakest part of the analysis. The same world price change applies everywhere, as if supply and the pass-through of world prices to farmers were the same in every country. Country effects are held at their 2016–2020 average, and some small neighboring countries are pooled into regions. In addition, each grid cell's revenue weights crops by the crop mix of its broad agro-ecological zone, rather than the cell's own crop mix. This reduces the palm response in palm frontiers such as Sumatra and Borneo and spreads it into Central Africa, which likely explains why the Democratic Republic of the Congo ranks first.
- We only count forest biomass carbon, and not peat, soil carbon, or lost future sequestration. Peat alone accounted for 614 of the 1,086 Tg CO₂e in Chen et al.'s estimate [@chen2026, Table 1, p. 13], mostly in Indonesia and Malaysia. Rapeseed and sunflower are also not included in the model. Both of these omissions understate ILUC.
- The soybean price change uses an accounting share (0.353), rather than an estimated market response. The oil price shock also makes no adjustment for soybean meal, which overstates the shock.
- Prices jump once and stay at that level, and cleared forest never grows back ([Appendix B](#sec-land-use-model)).
- Our sensitivity analysis only captures the spread across Roberts & Schlenker's six specifications, and does not capture the other uncertainties listed above.

## Appendix A: Background {#background}

### The IMO Net-Zero Framework

In April 2025, the International Maritime Organization approved draft amendments to Annex VI of the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL) [@sturrup2026, p. 1] that would set greenhouse-gas fuel-intensity (GFI) targets for ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above. GFI is measured in well-to-wake g CO₂e/MJ, relative to a 2008 baseline of 93.3 [@seber2025, p. 1]. The Base target tightens from a 4% reduction in 2028 to a 30% reduction by 2035, while the stricter Direct Compliance target tightens from 17% to 43%. Ships above the Base target pay \$380 per tonne of excess CO₂e (Tier 2), and ships between the two targets pay \$100 per tonne (Tier 1) [@seber2025, pp. 1–2].

As of October 2026, the framework has not been adopted. At an extraordinary session in October 2025, a Saudi Arabian motion to adjourn for one year passed with 57 votes, including 15 countries that had supported the framework in April [@carbonbrief2026]. The IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) met for its 84th session (MEPC 84) from 27 April to 1 May 2026. It kept the April 2025 text as the basis for further work, invited alternative proposals, and scheduled two more meetings of its Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG) [@carbonbrief2026; @abs2026mepc84, p. 4]. The first of these meetings, ISWG-GHG 22 (1–4 September 2026), ended without agreement [@shipandbunker2026]. The largest disagreement is over the greenhouse-gas (GHG) price and the central IMO fund it would pay into. According to one observer's count of the countries that spoke, 38 supported the price and fund and 17 (mostly oil producers) opposed them, while the United States again rejected any IMO-run fund [@shipandbunker2026]. The early GFI trajectory and the rules for pooling compliance surpluses are also unresolved [@maritimeexecutive2026]. Japan's proposal to replace the fund with direct payments from shipowners received little support in September [@maritimeexecutive2026]. Its revised proposal drops the fund and instead has ships cover shortfalls by buying surplus units from other ships [@marineinsight2026].

The working group meets again 23–27 November, followed by MEPC 85 (30 November–3 December). If MEPC 85 agrees, the extraordinary session will resume on 4 December 2026 and could vote that day [@abs2026mepc84, p. 4; @shipandbunker2026]. Whatever is adopted may differ from the April 2025 text that this analysis is based on. For example, a less stringent early trajectory would mean less biofuel demand, and dropping the GHG price would change the compliance costs that determine the fuel mix.

The framework only considers the direct life-cycle emissions of fuels. The IMO's life-cycle guidelines consider ILUC too uncertain to assign each fuel a value, and instead handle it through a qualitative, risk-based approach [@imo2024lca, paras. 4.12–4.13]. MEPC 84 supported this approach in principle and asked for more quantitative analysis by MEPC 85 [@abs2026mepc84, p. 6]. Since blending biofuel costs less than the \$380 Tier 2 penalty, the least-cost strategy is to blend just enough biofuel to meet the Base target. In ICCT's least-cost mix, used-cooking-oil renewable diesel (UCO-RD) runs out at about 5% of shipping energy, and virgin vegetable-oil renewable diesel (VO-RD) covers the rest, reaching 46% of shipping energy by 2035 [@seber2025, p. 4 and Table 1, p. 5].

ICCT's Table 1 gives the fuel mix for each year from 2028 to 2035. We read this table directly from the ICCT PDF. Its last column, virgin vegetable-oil feedstock, is the demand shift we use in this analysis. ICCT converts renewable diesel to vegetable oil at a rate of 1.22 kg of oil per kg of fuel [@seber2025, p. 3, note 9].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-icct-table-1

# icct_table_1 is read from ICCT's PDF in the inputs chunk.
knitr::kable(
  icct_table_1 |>
    dplyr::select(
      year,
      shipping_energy_demand_ej,
      base_target_trajectory_gco2e_mj,
      ucord_pct_energy_demand,
      vord_pct_energy_demand,
      vord_billion_liters,
      vo_demand_billion_liters
    ),
  col.names = c(
    "Year",
    "Shipping energy (EJ)",
    "Base target (g CO₂e/MJ)",
    "UCO-RD (% of energy)",
    "VO-RD (% of energy)",
    "VO-RD fuel (billion L)",
    "Virgin VO feedstock (billion L)"
  ),
  caption = "ICCT Table 1, selected columns [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. Virgin vegetable-oil feedstock, the last column, is the demand shock D."
)
```

@tbl-direct-ci shows the direct carbon intensities behind this fuel mix.

| Heavy fuel oil (HFO) | 92.8 |

None of these values include indirect land-use change. {#tbl-direct-ci}

### Published ILUC estimates

Published ILUC estimates for vegetable-oil biofuels vary widely (@tbl-published-iluc).

| Source | Approach | ILUC result |
|---|---|---|
| ICCT climate & revenue brief [@sturrup2026, pp. 10–11] | Fixed factor applied to ICCT's demand projection | 62 g CO₂e/MJ; ~285 Mt CO₂e/yr by 2035; ~950 Mt CO₂e over 2028–2035 |
| U.S. EPA model comparison [@epa2023mce, Table 7.7-1, p. 113] | Five models, soybean-oil biodiesel shock | Land-use change: 10 to 295 kg CO₂e/MMBTU (GCAM: 62) |
| @chen2026 [Table 1, p. 13] | Econometric estimates of demand → price → deforestation for palm, 2002–2018 | 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ (90% confidence interval 48.7–113.5) |
| Global Biosphere Management Model (GLOBIOM) for the EU [@valin2015, p. x] | Global economic land-use model, emissions spread over 20 years | 231 g CO₂e/MJ for palm oil, 150 for soybean oil |

: ICCT takes its 62 g CO₂e/MJ value from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) model comparison [@sturrup2026, p. 10]. The only value of 62 in the EPA's results table is the land-use-change value from the Global Change Analysis Model (GCAM), which is in kg CO₂e per million British thermal units (MMBTU) (≈ 59 g CO₂e/MJ), so we assume this is the source. Every value here is ILUC alone, without the fuel's direct emissions. ICCT adds its 62, weighted by VO-RD's share of shipping energy (62 × 46% ≈ 28.5 g CO₂e/MJ in 2035), to the fleet's Base-target GFI [@sturrup2026, pp. 10–11]. This puts the ILUC-adjusted fleet GFI at 93.86 g CO₂e/MJ in 2035, which is above the fossil baseline [@sturrup2026, Table A1, p. 15]. {#tbl-published-iluc}

## Appendix B: Methods and assumptions {#methods-and-assumptions}

This appendix describes each step of the analysis (@fig-steps) in more detail.

### From demand to a price shock {#sec-price-shock}

When demand shifts outward, the price rises by roughly the size of the demand shift divided by the difference between the supply and demand elasticities [@roberts2013, Table 1, panel C, p. 2279]:

$$ \%\Delta P \;\approx\; \underbrace{\frac{D}{Q_0}}_{\text{demand shift}} \;\times\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{\varepsilon_s - \varepsilon_d}}_{\text{multiplier } M} $$

where $D$ is virgin vegetable-oil demand for marine biofuel and $Q_0$ is baseline world production. The supply elasticity $\varepsilon_s > 0$ is the percentage increase in production when prices rise by 1%, and the demand elasticity $\varepsilon_d < 0$ is the percentage change in consumption. The multiplier $M$ is the percentage price increase for each percentage point of demand shift. The less that supply and demand respond to price, the larger the multiplier.

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Virgin vegetable-oil demand for marine biofuel, 2035 ($D$) | 139.3 billion L | ICCT [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5] |
| Baseline market ($Q_0$) | ≈ 204 Mt: world production of palm, soybean, rapeseed and sunflowerseed oil, 2024/25 | U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Production, Supply and Distribution (PSD) database [@usdapsd] |
| Oil density, to put $D$ and $Q_0$ in the same units | 0.92 kg/L | ICCT's own soy-oil conversion: 12.4 Mt = 13.5 billion L (0.919 kg/L) [@seber2025, Table A1, p. 7] |
| Supply elasticity ($\varepsilon_s$) | `r fmt_el(eps_s_rs)` (low end `r fmt_el(rs_low$eps_s)`, high end `r fmt_el(rs_high$eps_s)`) | @roberts2013 [Table 1, p. 2279]: about the average of their six specifications, which range from `r fmt_el(min(rs_specs$eps_s))` to `r fmt_el(max(rs_specs$eps_s))` |
| Demand elasticity ($\varepsilon_d$) | `r fmt_el(eps_d_rs)` (low end `r fmt_el(rs_low$eps_d)`, high end `r fmt_el(rs_high$eps_d)`) | @roberts2013 [Table 1, p. 2279]: about the average of their six specifications, which range from `r fmt_el(max(rs_specs$eps_d))` to `r fmt_el(min(rs_specs$eps_d))` |
| Demand year | 2035 only | Our choice: the final year of the ICCT projection |
| "Beyond marginal" flag | demand share > 25% | Our own cutoff for where the approximation gets unreliable (not from a source) |

: Inputs to the price shock. The central multiplier is $M \approx$ `r fmt1(m_rs)`; the low and high ends use `r fmt1(rs_low$m)` and `r fmt1(rs_high$m)`. {#tbl-price-shock-inputs}

$Q_0$ is the world production of the four oils in 2024/25, summed across countries using USDA's PSD oilseeds data downloaded on 31 July 2026 [@usdapsd]. Since USDA continuously revises the PSD data, a later download may differ slightly.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q0

# psd_four_oils is computed in the inputs chunk.
knitr::kable(
  psd_four_oils,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Commodity", "World production, 2024/25 (million t)"),
  caption = paste0(
    "World production of the four major vegetable oils (USDA PSD). Total: ",
    round(sum(psd_four_oils$production_mt), 1),
    " million t."
  )
)
```

Some notes on these choices:

- Vegetable oils substitute for one another, so we treat them as a single market, even though ships would burn soy oil [@chen2026, p. 4]. Roberts & Schlenker's elasticities describe the world market for calories from maize, wheat, rice, and soybeans, and we use them as a proxy for vegetable oils.
- Roberts & Schlenker estimate supply and demand together using six specifications: instrumental variables (IV) and three-stage least squares (3SLS), each with 3, 4, or 5 spline knots [@roberts2013, Table 1, p. 2279]. For the sensitivity analysis, we rerun everything with the two specifications that give the smallest and largest multiplier. We keep each specification's supply and demand elasticities together, rather than pairing the extremes of each range (@tbl-price-shock-check).
- We keep the supply elasticity in the multiplier because the emLab model takes prices as given, so the price we provide should already reflect the supply response. Dropping the supply elasticity would give $M = 20$ and triple the price shock.
- The formula is a linear approximation, and vegetable-oil demand for marine biofuel becomes a large share of the market from about 2032 onward. The 2035 price shock should therefore be interpreted as the likely scale of the effect, rather than its exact size. Roberts & Schlenker also note that, when accounting for uncertainty in the elasticities, the expected multiplier is higher than the one from their central estimates [@roberts2013, p. 2280].
- Roberts & Schlenker's supply elasticity is the output response to the price expected at planting, one year ahead. They argue it is not just a short-run lower bound, because farmers expect price changes to persist [@roberts2013, p. 2285]. Oil palm, however, takes about four years to start producing fruit [@chen2026, p. 4].
- Crushing soybeans also produces meal, and meal revenue relieves some of the pressure on oil prices. Roberts & Schlenker reduce their price effect by a third when a third of the calories return as animal feed [@roberts2013, p. 2280]. We do not make this adjustment, so our price shock is too high in this respect.
- Using Roberts & Schlenker's elasticities, the formula reproduces their headline price effect (@tbl-price-shock-check).

@tbl-price-shock-check shows Roberts & Schlenker's six specifications and the resulting multipliers, and @tbl-price-shock shows the price shock for each year from 2028 to 2035.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-price-shock-check
# Check: Roberts & Schlenker's ethanol mandate used about 5% of world calories (p. 2277), which they
# estimate raised prices about 30% (p. 2280). The formula should recover that from their elasticities.
ethanol_shift_pct <- 5
rs_table <- rbind(
  data.frame(spec = "Central values (primary scenario)", eps_s = eps_s_rs, eps_d = eps_d_rs, m = m_rs),
  rs_specs
)
rs_table$spec <- ifelse(
  rs_table$spec == rs_low$spec, paste(rs_table$spec, "(low end)"),
  ifelse(rs_table$spec == rs_high$spec, paste(rs_table$spec, "(high end)"), rs_table$spec)
)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Specification" = rs_table$spec,
    "Supply elasticity" = fmt_el(rs_table$eps_s),
    "Demand elasticity" = fmt_el(rs_table$eps_d),
    "Multiplier M" = formatC(rs_table$m, format = "f", digits = 2),
    "Ethanol mandate: %ΔP from a 5% shift" = paste0(fmt0(ethanol_shift_pct * rs_table$m), "%"),
    "Marine biofuel: %ΔP in 2035" = paste0(fmt0(share_2035 * rs_table$m), "%"),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = "lrrrrr",
  caption = paste(
    "Roberts & Schlenker's six specifications [@roberts2013, Table 1, p. 2279] and the central values we",
    "use, about their average. The ethanol column checks the formula: their ethanol mandate used about 5%",
    "of world calories [@roberts2013, p. 2277], which they estimate raised prices about 30%",
    "[@roberts2013, p. 2280]. The low and high ends, the specifications with the smallest and largest",
    "multiplier, are our sensitivity runs."
  )
)
```

```{r}

knitr::kable(
  price_shock |>
    dplyr::mutate(beyond_marginal = ifelse(beyond_marginal, "yes", "")),
  digits = 1,

### Mapping the shock to the model's crops {#sec-mapping}

Following @chen2026 [p. 3], we apply the same percentage shock to all vegetable-oil prices. Palm oil prices respond to production shocks in competing oil crops about as strongly as to shocks in palm itself (their Fig. 2A, p. 4), and the four oil prices move together in the long run, almost one-for-one [cointegrating coefficients of 1.04 for soybean, 1.01 for canola, and 0.86 for sunflower oil, @chen2026, Table S5]. Other studies add nuance. @cui2017 [abstract] find that soy oil diverted to US biodiesel is replaced mostly by palm oil, and @santeramo2017 [p. 13] finds a mix of substitutes and complements that varies by oil and region. Allowing each oil's price to respond differently would be a sensible refinement.

Only two of the model's 17 crops produce vegetable oil: palm, which is priced per tonne of palm oil, and soybeans, which are priced per tonne of beans. According to the emLab model's code, their baseline prices are observed 2020 prices of \$768/t for palm and \$415/t for soybeans. Both are within 2% of the World Bank's 2020 averages (\$752/t and \$407/t). Soybean oil averaged \$838/t that year [@worldbank2022pink, p. 1].

| Model crop | Shock | Why | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Palm oil | $\%\Delta P$ | The model prices palm as oil | — |
| Soybeans | $s \times \%\Delta P$, with $s = 0.353$ | Oil is only part of a soybean's value, and we hold the meal price fixed. $s = \$4.72 / (\$4.72 + \$8.66)$, from the 2007–2025 average per-bushel values of soybean oil and meal | @janzen2025 [Fig. 2] (USDA Agricultural Marketing Service Illinois plant prices; 11 lb oil and 48 lb meal per bushel) |
| Rapeseed/canola, sunflower | not modeled | Not among the model's crops | — |

: How the oil-price shock enters the emLab model. {#tbl-crop-mapping}

We performed two checks on $s$. Irwin's 2007–2017 averages (\$4.43 for oil and \$8.33 for meal) give 0.347 [@irwin2017, Fig. 3], and World Bank 2020 prices (\$838/t for oil and \$394/t for meal) give 0.33 [@worldbank2022pink, p. 1]. The share varies from week to week. It ranged between 25% and 35% over 2013–2020, has rarely been below 35% since, and briefly reached 50% in 2021 and 2025 [@janzen2025, Fig. 3]. Note that $s$ is an accounting share, rather than an estimate of how soybean prices respond.

Rapeseed and sunflower are not in the model, so their land-use response is missing and ILUC is understated. We still define $Q_0$ using all four oils because they compete in a single market, and using only palm and soy would inflate the demand share. In 2024/25, 86% of world rapeseed came from Canada, the EU, China, India, Australia, and Russia, and 90% of sunflowerseed came from Russia, Ukraine, the EU, Argentina, Kazakhstan, and China [@usdapsd]. Most of the missing response is therefore probably outside of tropical forests, although we have not quantified it.

### The emLab land-use model {#sec-land-use-model}

We use emLab's global deforestation model without changes, except that its scenarios set crop prices rather than carbon prices.

The model is a statistical model of the share of each grid cell's forest cleared each year, as a function of the cell's potential agricultural revenue and its remaining tree cover. It is estimated using 2001–2020 data (29.1 million cell-years). It controls for each cell's fixed characteristics and for conditions in each country and year (i.e., a fractional logit with cell and country-by-year fixed effects). A cell's revenue is the crop price minus transport cost, multiplied by attainable yield. Revenue is averaged across the 17 crops based on their share of harvested area in the cell's agro-ecological zone, and converted to a present value using a 5% discount rate. Transport cost scales with travel time to port and the crude oil price.

Starting from 2020 tree cover, the model steps forward one year at a time until 2171, across 1,450,769 grid cells (1/12°, about 9 km across) in 154 countries. Country effects are held at their 2016–2020 average, and cleared forest never grows back.

All runs use a carbon price of zero, and BAU uses 2020 prices. The primary run raises palm oil prices by `r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`% and soybean prices by `r fmt1(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%. Two additional runs apply this shock to palm and soybeans separately, in order to split the loss by crop. For the sensitivity analysis, two more runs repeat the primary run using the price shocks at the low and high ends of Roberts & Schlenker's estimates (`r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_low)`% and `r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_high)`% for palm; see [Results](#sec-results-price)). Prices jump once in the first model year and stay at that level. Model year 2035 therefore means 15 years after the shock, rather than the calendar year 2035.

Forest carbon (t CO₂) is tree cover multiplied by carbon density, and forest area (ha) is carbon divided by density, using the model's own conversion. We count lost forest carbon as emissions, which leaves out peat, soil carbon, and lost future sequestration. As a sanity check, the model has `r fmt0(sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) / 1e6)` Mha of forest in 2020, which is `r fmt0(100 * sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) / 4.06e9)`% of the 4.06 billion ha estimated by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations [@fao2020fra, p. 1]. Note that the two sources define forest differently.

We use the model's input data without modification, and summarize its results by country and by 0.5° grid square. Map outlines are from Natural Earth's 1:110m countries dataset [@naturalearth].

### ILUC carbon intensity {#sec-iluc-method}

We spread the additional emissions over an accounting period of $T$ years of fuel use:

$$ \text{ILUC}_T = \frac{\Delta C(T)}{T \times E} $$

where $\Delta C(T)$ is the cumulative additional forest carbon loss $T$ years after the shock, and $E$ is one year of VO-RD energy at the 2035 level. This is ICCT's 46.0% VO-RD share of 10.0 EJ of shipping energy, or 4.60 EJ [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. Calculating this from the feedstock instead (139.3 billion L of oil at 0.92 kg/L, 1.22 kg of oil per kg of fuel, and 43,980 MJ per tonne of fuel) gives 4.62 EJ [@seber2025, pp. 3 and 6, Table A1]. Since the model applies the 2035 demand level from its first year, $T$ years means $T$ years of fuel use at that level, rather than a span of calendar years.

There is no standard value for $T$. The EU uses 20 years [@valin2015, p. 3] and the US EPA uses 30 years [@chen2026, p. 13]. We report 20, 25, and 30 years, and use 25 years for our headline value. This is the period Chen et al. use to match the oil palm replanting cycle [@chen2026, p. 13], so our value can be compared directly with their 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ. ICCT's 62 g CO₂e/MJ comes from the EPA's model comparison, which divides cumulative 2020–2050 emissions by cumulative fuel use over the same years [@epa2023mce, pp. 83–84], so it is most comparable to our 30-year value.

The result only counts CO₂ from forest biomass. We split it by country using each country's share of the additional loss, and by crop using the palm-only and soy-only runs.

## Use of generative AI

We used Claude (Anthropic, model Opus 5.5) through Claude Code as a coding and writing assistant. It drafted and edited much of the R code, including the changes to the emLab model's scenario inputs, and much of this report's prose, and it helped find and check sources. GitHub Copilot's coding agent set up the initial Quarto report and GitHub Pages workflow. We set the research question and scenarios, chose the data sources and key assumptions, and reviewed the code and text. The AI tools are not authors, and we are responsible for all code, analysis and conclusions. The AI tools produced no data or results: every number, figure and table is computed by the code in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/emlab-ucsb/marine-biofuel-iluc-prototype) when the report is built.
